paragraphs: Peter Benenson read a newspaper item about two Portuguese students jailed for raising a toast to freedom, and it moved him to act. In May 1961 he persuaded The Observer to give him space for an article, Appeal for Amnesty, naming eight forgotten prisoners held for their beliefs across different political systems, chosen deliberately to avoid taking one side in the Cold War.

The response, thousands of letters from readers, turned a single article into a standing organisation within the year. Amnesty International's method, letter-writing campaigns on behalf of named individuals, proved durable enough that it still headquarters in London and now covers well over a hundred countries. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.

Henry II did not invent the jury in 1166, but he made it routine. His Assize of Clarendon ordered twelve men from every hundred, and four from every village, to report under oath which of their neighbours were suspected of murder, robbery or theft, feeding accusations straight into the king's travelling justices rather than local lords' courts.

The assize also built the infrastructure that made royal justice stick: new gaols in counties that lacked one, and instructions for sheriffs on holding suspects for trial. It shifted criminal accusation away from private feud and church ordeal toward a state process, a change historians treat as one of the founding moments of English common law.

Cesare Beccaria was in his mid-twenties and largely unknown when he published On Crimes and Punishments anonymously in 1764, fearing reprisal from the Milanese authorities he was criticising. He argued that punishment should be swift, certain and proportionate rather than savage, and that torture produced false confessions, not truth.

The book was short, blunt and quickly translated across Europe. Voltaire wrote a commentary on it, Catherine the Great corresponded with Beccaria, and both Thomas Jefferson and John Adams copied long passages into their own notebooks, carrying its arguments directly into the drafting of American criminal law.

Before William Blackstone, English law lived mostly in judges' heads and centuries of scattered case reports. He began as Oxford's first professor of English law in the 1750s, and his lecture notes grew into Commentaries on the Laws of England, published in four volumes between 1765 and 1769.

The book sold enormously in the American colonies, where formal legal training was scarce, and lawyers there leaned on it as a working substitute for a proper library. Founders including John Adams and Alexander Hamilton cited it directly, and its structure and phrasing still surface in American case law more than two centuries later.

Before 1532, criminal justice across the Holy Roman Empire varied town by town, with no shared rules for evidence or punishment. The Constitutio Criminalis Carolina, agreed at Augsburg in 1530 and ratified at Regensburg two years later under Emperor Charles V, gave the empire its first common criminal procedure, including detailed rules for when judges could order torture.

The code was also, in its own limited way, a check on abuse: it required judges to base a torture order on prior evidence rather than suspicion alone, and it distinguished degrees of murder for the first time in German law. Local territories kept the right to apply harsher penalties of their own, so the Carolina set a floor rather than a ceiling.

Lipit-Ishtar ruled the city of Isin in the twentieth century BCE and had his laws carved in Sumerian, not Akkadian. That choice mattered: Sumerian was already fading as a spoken language, kept alive in schools and temples, so writing the code in it was a claim to old authority rather than a practical necessity for ordinary litigants.

The code survives mostly through student copies rather than a single monument, tablets on which trainee scribes practised their letters by transcribing the prologue and about forty surviving provisions. It covers slaves, boats, rented oxen and inheritance, and it is the second-oldest Mesopotamian law code known, after Ur-Nammu's, predating Hammurabi's more famous version by over a century.

Star Chamber began under Henry VII as a useful check on nobles too powerful for ordinary courts to touch, sitting without a jury and taking cases the common law struggled to reach. By the 1620s, under James I and then Charles I, it had turned into something closer to a political weapon, punishing pamphleteers and critics of royal policy with fines, mutilation and imprisonment.

Its name came from the star-patterned ceiling of the room it met in at Westminster, not from anything mystical. Parliament abolished the court outright in 1641, during the build-up to civil war, and Star Chamber became shorthand in English and American law for a proceeding conducted in secret with no real defence.

Labour backbencher Sidney Silverman had tried and failed for years to get capital punishment off the statute book before his private member's bill finally passed. The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act received royal assent on 8 November 1965, suspending hanging for murder in Great Britain for five years in the first instance, with Parliament required to vote again before it lapsed.

That renewal vote came in 1969 and made the suspension permanent, though Northern Ireland kept the death penalty for murder until 1973, and it remained on the books for a handful of other offences, such as treason, until 1998. The last executions in Britain, of Peter Allen and Gwynne Evans, had taken place in August 1964, before the act was even law.

Sixteen lawyers under the jurist Tribonian were given an almost unmanageable task: read through around three million lines written by thirty-nine earlier Roman jurists and compress the usable law into a single reference work. They finished in December 533, faster than expected, producing fifty books built from over nine thousand extracted passages.

Each extract kept its original author's name attached, so a judge citing the Digest was still, technically, citing centuries-old opinions rather than a new statute. It became one of four parts of what later scholars called the Corpus Juris Civilis, and copies of it, rediscovered and studied intensively in medieval Italy, gave European universities the base text on which continental civil law was rebuilt.

Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish artillery captain, had been convicted of passing military secrets to Germany in 1894 on forged evidence and shipped to a penal colony in French Guiana. A second officer's forgeries eventually exposed the fraud, and Emile Zola's open letter accusing the army of a cover-up split French opinion for years.

A retrial in 1899 convicted him again, absurdly, with mitigating circumstances, and France's president pardoned him days later rather than reopen the wound further. He was not formally exonerated by the courts until 1906, and the affair left a lasting fracture between the French army, the Church and republican politics.

Israeli agents seized Adolf Eichmann off a street in Buenos Aires in May 1960, where he had been living under a false name for a decade, and flew him to Jerusalem to face trial. He had run the Reich Security Main Office section that scheduled the deportation of Jews to camps across occupied Europe, work he later described as routine administration.

The trial opened in April 1961 in a Jerusalem theatre converted for the purpose, and survivor witnesses gave testimony broadcast live, many hearing their own history spoken aloud in a courtroom for the first time. Eichmann sat behind bulletproof glass and argued he had merely followed orders. Convicted of crimes against humanity, he was hanged in June 1962, the only civil execution Israel has ever carried out.

The court sat for the first time in 1959, created to enforce a convention the Council of Europe had signed a decade earlier, and it opened for business in Strasbourg with a handful of judges hearing barely any cases at all. For its first years, individuals could not even bring complaints directly; only states and a screening commission could refer a case forward.

That changed over subsequent decades as more countries accepted the right of individual petition, and the court's docket grew accordingly, eventually into the tens of thousands of applications a year. Its rulings bind member states but carry no independent enforcement power beyond the political weight of the Council of Europe, which has occasionally suspended a state's membership over noncompliance.

In 1908 Attorney General Charles Bonaparte, a great-nephew of Napoleon, created a small standing force of federal investigators inside the Justice Department, over objections from Congress, which distrusted the idea of a national police force answerable to the executive. It began with under forty agents and no name that stuck for years, known first simply as the Bureau of Investigation.

It was renamed the Federal Bureau of Investigation in 1935, by which point J. Edgar Hoover, its director since 1924, had already reshaped it around standardised training, a fingerprint file and relentless publicity. Hoover would run it for another thirty-seven years, longer than any FBI director before or since.

Francisca Rojas's two children were found dead in her home near Necochea, Argentina, in June 1892, and she blamed a neighbour. A police investigator named Alvarez, trained in the fingerprint classification system Juan Vucetich had been developing at La Plata, found a bloody thumbprint on a door and matched it to Rojas herself.

Confronted with the print, she confessed. It was the first murder conviction built on fingerprint evidence anywhere in the world, and it vindicated a method Vucetich had spent barely a year refining. Argentina adopted his system nationally within a decade, ahead of the fingerprint bureaus Britain and the United States were still building.

London's uniformed police had existed since 1829, but by the 1840s Scotland Yard's leadership accepted that a man in a tall hat and blue coat could not catch a pickpocket who saw him coming a street away. In 1842 they formed a small detective branch, initially just two inspectors and six sergeants working in plain clothes.

The idea was controversial: critics worried that officers who did not announce themselves as police were little better than spies on the public. The branch grew anyway, and by the 1870s had become the Criminal Investigation Department, a model that police forces in other countries copied over the following decades.

Eastern State Penitentiary opened outside Philadelphia in 1829 built on a wagon-wheel plan of radiating cell blocks, then the largest and most expensive public building in the United States. Each prisoner lived and worked alone, with a small exercise yard attached to the cell, on the theory that isolation with a Bible would produce genuine penitence.

Prisoners wore hoods when moved through the halls so they could never see another inmate's face, and guards padded the corridors in socks to keep even footsteps from breaking the silence. The regime drew visitors including Charles Dickens, who condemned it as crueller than physical punishment, and the total-isolation model was largely abandoned by the century's end.

The 1850 law was part of a compromise meant to hold the Union together, and it went far beyond earlier fugitive slave statutes. It denied accused runaways a jury trial, barred their testimony in their own defence, and made federal marshals who failed to arrest them liable to a fine.

Ordinary Northern citizens could now be compelled to join a hunt for an escaped person and pay for refusing, and free Black people were seized on false claims with no hearing to contest them. The backlash radicalised abolitionist opinion across the North and hardened the sectional divide that led to war within the decade.

Almost nothing personal is known about Gaius himself, not even his family name, only that he was writing legal teaching material in the Roman provinces around 161 CE. His Institutes organised Roman law into four books, covering persons, property, obligations and legal procedure, a structure clear enough that later Roman law students learned the subject in that order for generations.

The text was thought lost until 1816, when scholars in Verona found it underneath later religious writing on a reused parchment, a palimpsest where monks had scraped away the original ink to reuse the page. That accidental survival gave Justinian's compilers, working in the 530s, a working model to imitate when they built their own Institutes, so a provincial teaching manual ended up shaping the backbone of European civil law.

The General Data Protection Regulation took effect across the European Union on 25 May 2018, four years after Brussels first proposed it, and applied to any company handling the data of EU residents regardless of where that company was based. Consent for collecting personal data had to be specific and freely given, not buried in a pre-ticked box, and users gained a formal right to see, correct or delete what a company held on them.

Fines for breaches could reach 4 percent of a company's global annual revenue, a figure large enough that firms worldwide rewrote privacy policies and cookie banners in the months before the deadline rather than risk it. Several other jurisdictions, including California and Brazil, drafted their own laws afterwards using GDPR's structure as the starting template.

Raphael Lemkin, a Polish Jewish lawyer who had coined the word genocide in 1944, spent years lobbying delegates one by one to get this convention onto the General Assembly's agenda. It passed on 9 December 1948, a day before the Universal Declaration, and defined genocide narrowly: acts committed with intent to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The convention obliged signing states to prevent and punish genocide, but wrote in no enforcement mechanism of its own. That gap mattered: it took until the 1990s, with tribunals for the former Yugoslavia and Rwanda, for anyone to be convicted of the crime it named. The United States did not ratify the treaty until 1988, forty years after adopting it.

Clarence Earl Gideon had an eighth-grade education and a string of minor convictions when Florida charged him with breaking into a Panama City pool hall in 1961. He asked the judge for a lawyer he could not afford and was refused, because state law only appointed counsel in capital cases. Gideon defended himself, was convicted, and wrote his appeal to the Supreme Court by hand from his prison cell.

The Court ruled unanimously on 18 March 1963 that the Sixth Amendment right to counsel applies to defendants in state courts too, overturning its own 1942 precedent in Betts v Brady. Florida retried Gideon with a real defence lawyer, and he was acquitted. The case became the reason every American facing serious criminal charges is entitled to a public defender if they cannot pay for one.

The text runs across twelve columns cut into a curved wall, reading in boustrophedon: the lines alternate direction, right to left then left to right, like a plough turning at the end of a furrow. It was reused as building material in a Roman odeum, which is why it survived at all, and it was only recognised for what it was when excavated at Gortyn on Crete in 1884.

Its rules on inheritance are unusually specific for the fifth century BCE: a daughter inherited half of what a son received, but town houses, farm equipment and livestock were carved out of her share entirely. It also set procedures for divorce, adoption and disputes between free and enslaved people, and its survival intact makes it the fullest legal text to reach us from the ancient Greek world.

Church law before 1140 was a scattered mess of council rulings, papal letters and forged decrees, many contradicting each other outright. A Bologna monk known only as Gratian gathered roughly 3,800 of these texts into the Concordia discordantium canonum, arranging apparent contradictions into questions and then resolving them with his own commentary.

Bologna already hosted Europe's first law school, and Gratian's book became its core canon law text almost immediately, studied alongside Roman civil law. It stayed the backbone of Catholic legal education for over seven centuries, until the Vatican finally replaced it with a formal Code of Canon Law in 1917.

No copy of the Yassa has ever been found, and historians still argue whether it was one unified code at all. What survives comes from later chroniclers describing rules Genghis Khan issued piecemeal after 1206: death for theft, desertion or failing to help a fallen comrade in battle, and religious tolerance across a fast-growing empire of many faiths.

The Secret History of the Mongols says Genghis ordered his adopted son Shigi Qutuqu to keep a written register of judgments in a blue script, kept away from ordinary subjects and consulted only by the khan's inner circle. That secrecy is precisely why nothing verifiable remains beyond fragments quoted decades later by Persian and Mongol writers.

The first detainees arrived at Camp X-Ray, a hastily built cage of chain-link cells at the US naval base on Cuba, on 11 January 2002, flown in from Afghanistan in the months after the September 11 attacks. The administration chose the base partly because it sits outside the continental United States, arguing detainees there fell outside the reach of ordinary American courts.

That argument did not hold: in 2004 and 2008 the Supreme Court ruled that prisoners held there could challenge their detention through habeas corpus. Hundreds passed through the camp over the following two decades, many held for years without charge, and reports of interrogation methods including waterboarding drew sustained international criticism. Promises by successive presidents to close it went unfulfilled.

A highwayman named Nicolas Jacques Pelletier went to the scaffold in Paris on 25 April 1792, the first person executed by the machine that would define the Revolution. It had been designed at the request of Dr Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, who argued that a blade gave every condemned person, noble or commoner, the same quick death.

Before it, executions varied by class and crime: beheading by sword for the wealthy, hanging or breaking on the wheel for the poor. The new device removed that distinction and, within two years, was carrying out thousands of executions during the Terror, making its inventor's name a byword he had never wanted.

Death was the default penalty in Hammurabi's Babylon for a huge range of offences, but the roughly two hundred laws recorded on tablets from the Hittite capital Hattusa reach for it in only a handful of cases. Killing a man in a quarrel could be settled by handing over dependants as compensation instead of a life for a life.

Later copies of the tablets show scribes actively revising older, harsher versions downward, replacing an earlier death sentence with a fine, which is rare evidence of a legal system consciously softening itself over time rather than merely accumulating rulings. Mutilation was largely reserved for slaves caught in theft or arson, while free Hittites paid in silver, sheep or land instead.

The Rome Statute that created the court had been adopted in 1998, but it needed sixty countries to ratify it before it could take effect, a threshold reached in April 2002. The court itself opened in The Hague that July, the first permanent tribunal with standing jurisdiction over genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and, later, aggression, rather than one convened after a specific conflict.

It can only act when a country will not or cannot prosecute a case itself, and it has no police force of its own to make arrests. The United States, Russia and China never joined, and its early caseload was criticised for focusing almost entirely on Africa. Its first verdict, convicting Congolese militia leader Thomas Lubanga, came only in 2012.

Vienna's police president Johannes Schober convened delegates from twenty countries in September 1923, arguing that criminals crossing borders by rail and telegraph had outpaced any single force's ability to chase them. The meeting created the International Criminal Police Commission, with Vienna as its base.

The organisation survived the Second World War only in name, its files and leadership largely taken over by Nazi Germany after 1938, and it had to be effectively rebuilt from Paris afterward. It took the name Interpol, already its telegraph code, as its official title in 1956, and now coordinates police cooperation among more than 190 member countries.

The Fourth Lateran Council's 1215 ban on clergy blessing ordeals left English courts with no way to determine guilt in serious criminal cases. King Henry III's judges spent the next few years improvising, and by 1219 royal instructions told justices to convene juries of local men to decide questions of fact instead.

The switch was pragmatic rather than principled: juries were already used to bring accusations under Henry II's earlier reforms, so extending them to verdicts was a small step rather than an invention. It set England on a legal path distinct from continental Europe, where inquisitorial procedure and judicial torture filled the gap the ordeal left behind.

Every other post-Roman kingdom wrote its laws in Latin. Aethelberht of Kent did not: his code survives only in a twelfth-century copy called the Textus Roffensis, but its ninety short clauses are the oldest surviving text in the English language, older than any English poem, charter or chronicle known.

The clauses read like a price list. Cutting off someone's ear cost six shillings, breaking a thigh twelve, and compensation scaled by rank all the way up to the king himself. It was compiled shortly after Augustine's mission reached Kent in 597, and church officials were slotted into the existing scale of fines rather than given a new one of their own.

The kingdom of Eshnunna, on the Diyala river near modern Baghdad, produced the earliest known law code written in Akkadian rather than Sumerian. Two tablets, found decades apart and only later recognised as copies of the same text, opened with fixed prices for barley, oil, wool and the hire of a wagon or an ox, before moving on to theft, assault and marriage.

Its penalties are strikingly proportional: a bitten-off nose or ear carried a set silver fine, and a slave's misdeed cost its owner less than a free man's own. It predates Hammurabi's code, issued at Babylon roughly a century and a half later, and the overlap between the two suggests Hammurabi's scribes knew and reused earlier Mesopotamian legal tradition rather than inventing it from nothing.

Nathan Leopold and Richard Loeb were nineteen and eighteen, both from wealthy Chicago families and both university graduates already, when they murdered fourteen-year-old Bobby Franks in 1924 for no reason either could explain beyond wanting to commit a perfect crime. A pair of eyeglasses dropped near the body led police to Leopold within days.

Their families hired Clarence Darrow, who avoided a jury entirely by pleading them guilty and arguing for mercy directly to the judge across a twelve-hour closing speech. It worked: both were sentenced to life plus ninety-nine years rather than hanged, a result that scandalised a public expecting an execution for a crime committed for pure intellectual thrill.

Passed sometime in the third century BCE, the law took its name from the tribune Aquilius and dealt with damnum iniuria datum, damage inflicted without right, covering everything from a trampled crop to a slave or grazing animal killed outright. It set damages at the highest value the property had reached in the previous year, rather than its worth at the moment it was destroyed.

If a defendant denied liability in court and the judge found against him anyway, the compensation doubled, which discouraged frivolous denial. The law could only order a payment, never the replacement of the animal or slave itself, and jurists kept refining its wording for centuries; Justinian's compilers were still quoting and glossing it more than seven hundred years later.

The Twelve Tables, drawn up only five years earlier, had explicitly banned marriage between patricians and plebeians for the first time in writing, turning a social convention into law. The tribune Gaius Canuleius proposed reversing it in 445 BCE, and patrician consuls fought him hard, warning that mixed marriages would corrupt Rome's bloodlines and its social order.

Plebeians eventually forced the issue by refusing to serve in the army while the city faced hostile neighbours, a tactic they had already used once before. Canuleius's marriage law passed, though his attempt to open the consulship itself to plebeians did not; as a compromise Rome instead created military tribunes with consular power, a post either order could hold.

Clovis, the first king to unite the Frankish tribes, had their customary law written down between about 507 and 511, covering theft, injury and family property in plain, itemised clauses rather than Roman-style legal reasoning. Most of it dealt with everyday disputes and set fines in silver for specific injuries, down to the price of a broken finger.

One clause barred a woman from inheriting a particular category of family farmland, a narrow rule about property, not thrones. When French jurists excluded women from the crown after 1316 and again in 1328, they argued from other principles entirely; no source shows anyone citing this old Frankish text at the time. Only later, retroactively, did the name Salic Law attach itself to that royal exclusion.

Proposed by the tribune Lucius Villius in 180 BCE, this law fixed a minimum age for each rung of the Roman career ladder rather than leaving it to custom: roughly thirty for the quaestorship, thirty-six for the aedileship, thirty-nine for the praetorship and forty-two for the consulship. It also required years of prior military service before a young Roman could stand for any of them.

The law is thought to have added a mandatory gap year, or biennium, between holding one curule office and standing for the next, slowing ambitious careers deliberately. Ages drifted afterward as individual exceptions were granted, most famously to generals the senate wanted in command early, but the ladder Villius set became the reference point every later debate over Roman office measured itself against.

Charles Lindbergh's twenty-month-old son had been taken from his New Jersey nursery in 1932 and found dead weeks later, a crime that drew national obsession because of the father's fame as the first man to fly the Atlantic solo. Bruno Richard Hauptmann, a German-born carpenter, was arrested in 1934 after some of the ransom money turned up traced to him.

His 1935 trial in Flemington, New Jersey, drew hundreds of reporters and was covered almost like a sporting event, with H.L. Mencken calling it the biggest story since the Resurrection. Hauptmann was convicted largely on circumstantial evidence, including a ladder allegedly built from wood in his attic, and was executed in 1936; doubts about the verdict persist among historians.

Magdeburg's town charter, granted in the twelfth century, let citizens elect their own council, run their own court and set their own market rules instead of answering to a feudal lord. By 1300 that template had spread east through German settlement into Poland, Bohemia, Silesia and beyond, adopted by hundreds of towns that wanted the same independence.

A town did not need a Magdeburg official present to adopt the law, only a copy of its written rulings, so the code travelled far faster than any army could. Krakow, Vilnius and dozens of other cities ran on versions of Magdeburg rights well into the eighteenth century, long after Magdeburg itself had lost any special influence over them.

William Marbury sued over a routine judicial commission that the outgoing administration had signed but never delivered before Thomas Jefferson took office in 1801. It looked like a minor paperwork dispute, not the case that would define the American judiciary.

Chief Justice John Marshall ruled in 1803 that Marbury had a right to the commission but that the law letting him sue directly in the Supreme Court was itself unconstitutional. In striking down that law, the court claimed for itself the power to void acts of Congress, a power the Constitution had never explicitly granted it.

The founding Ming emperor, Zhu Yuanzhang, had risen from a peasant rebel to ruler and distrusted the bureaucracy he now commanded. His Great Ming Code, finalised in 1397 after several earlier drafts, laid out punishments by exact rank and offence, from beating with a light bamboo cane up to strangulation and decapitation for the gravest crimes.

It borrowed structure from the earlier Tang code but tightened penalties for officials who abused their positions, reflecting Zhu's obsession with corruption. The code stayed in force through the rest of the Ming dynasty and supplied the template the following Qing dynasty adapted for its own criminal law, extending its influence to nearly three hundred years after Zhu's death.

Edward I's parliament of 1275 passed a single act with over fifty clauses, covering everything from wool export duties to how quickly a rape victim had to raise the alarm. It was among the first English statutes written down and preserved as a distinct, numbered law rather than folded loosely into a judge's private notes.

Historians call it the First Statute of Westminster to distinguish it from a second one Edward issued in 1285. Together they restated and tightened Magna Carta's older promises, and later English lawyers treated the 1275 statute as settled precedent, citing its clauses in courtrooms for centuries after Edward's death.

The biblical account puts this at Mount Sinai in the wake of the exodus from Egypt, traditionally dated to around 1300 BCE, though no archaeological find independently confirms an exodus of that scale or fixes the mountain's location. The commandments are recorded twice, in Exodus and again in Deuteronomy, with small differences in wording between the two versions that later rabbis and translators had to reconcile.

Jewish and Christian tradition count the commandments differently: Judaism treats the opening declaration of divine identity as the first, while most Christian traditions fold it into a preface and split a later verse on coveting into two. The text itself never numbers them, so the familiar list of ten is an interpretive convention laid over Hebrew scripture rather than a count the original gives.

The defendants confessed. That was the point: three public trials in Moscow between 1936 and 1938 paraded former Bolshevik leaders, including Grigory Zinoviev and Nikolai Bukharin, into court to admit, on record, to plots against Stalin that had never occurred. Confessions came after months in NKVD custody, often extracted under torture or threats to family.

Foreign journalists and diplomats watched from the gallery, and several came away persuaded the confessions were genuine, an outcome the Kremlin had designed the theatre to produce. Almost every defendant was shot within days of sentencing. The trials gave the wider Great Purge a legal veneer, turning the disappearance of Stalin's rivals into something that looked, on paper, like justice.

A white Ford Bronco crawling down a Los Angeles freeway, trailed by police cars and helicopters, opened the case to television before a single witness had testified. O.J. Simpson, a former NFL running back turned broadcaster, was charged with murdering his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman, and the trial that followed ran for months and was carried live almost daily.

The defence built its case around police mishandling of evidence and the racial history of the LAPD, undercutting a glove that prosecutors had presented as damning when Simpson tried it on and it appeared not to fit. The jury acquitted him on 3 October 1995 after less than four hours of deliberation, a verdict that split American public opinion sharply along racial lines.

The case against the Pendle families began with a chance encounter on a Lancashire road. A pedlar refused to sell pins to Alizon Device, she cursed him, he collapsed, and her own confession to causing it dragged in her mother, brother and grandmother, then a rival family the Chattoxes.

Twelve people stood trial at Lancaster Assizes in August 1612. Ten were hanged at Gallows Hill on 20 August, one of the largest single witchcraft executions in English history and unusually well recorded, because the court clerk Thomas Potts published a detailed account, The Wonderfull Discoverie of Witches, within months of the verdicts.

Daniel Ellsberg, a defence analyst who had worked on a secret Pentagon history of the Vietnam War, photocopied thousands of its pages and passed them to the New York Times. The Nixon administration went to court to stop publication, arguing national security, and won a temporary injunction, the first time a US court had ever blocked a newspaper before publication on those grounds.

The Supreme Court heard the case on an emergency basis and ruled 6 to 3 on 30 June 1971 that the government had not met the heavy burden required to justify prior restraint on the press. The papers, which showed officials had misled the public about the war's progress for years, resumed publication days later. The ruling became a foundation of American press freedom law.

Charles I had raised money without Parliament through a forced loan in 1626 and jailed men who refused to pay it, including five knights who challenged their imprisonment as a breach of habeas corpus and lost. Parliament answered in 1628 with the Petition of Right, demanding no taxation without its consent, no imprisonment without cause shown, and no billeting of soldiers in private homes.

Charles gave an evasive first answer, and only signed properly worded assent when the Commons withheld a badly needed subsidy. He treated the petition as a one-off concession rather than a lasting limit, but it became one of the documents later cited alongside Magna Carta as a foundation of English constitutional rights.

Allan Pinkerton was a Chicago barrel maker and abolitionist before he became a detective, drawn into the work after helping break up a counterfeiting ring near his home. In 1850 he founded the North-Western Police Agency, soon renamed Pinkerton National Detective Agency, and built a client list that included railroads with no local police jurisdiction to call on.

The agency later ran an early Secret Service style unit protecting Abraham Lincoln and, in the following decades, made itself infamous strikebreaking against labour unions, most violently at Homestead in 1892. At its peak it reportedly employed more agents than the standing US Army, operating across state lines federal law enforcement had not yet been built to cover.

Rome had managed with a single praetor for over a century, but 242 BCE, near the end of the First Punic War, brought enough foreign merchants and disputes into the city that the senate created a second one solely for cases involving non-citizens. The existing praetor kept jurisdiction over Roman citizens; the new praetor peregrinus took everything else.

Because no fixed Roman statute covered a dispute between a Carthaginian trader and a Greek one, this praetor had to reason from principles both sides could be expected to recognise rather than from citizen-only civil law. That improvised body of shared rules became known as the ius gentium, the law of peoples, and it fed directly into how later Roman jurists thought about universal legal principle.

The code that Qin imposed on China after unification in 221 BCE had roots a century earlier in reforms the statesman Shang Yang pushed through for the Qin state alone. Its core idea was equality of a harsh kind: punishments were written down, published, and applied the same way regardless of rank, replacing the older system where nobles answered to custom and commoners to a magistrate's discretion.

Households were grouped into units of five or ten and made collectively liable, so a neighbour's crime could bring punishment on people who had done nothing themselves. That pressure helped Qin's armies and bureaucracy outperform rival states, but the same harshness applied across a much larger unified empire provoked revolts within years of the First Emperor's death, and the dynasty collapsed within a generation.

The killing in Rwanda began on 7 April 1994 and had run its course within about a hundred days, leaving roughly 800,000 people dead, most of them Tutsi. The United Nations Security Council responded that November, passing Resolution 955 to create a tribunal with the authority to prosecute those responsible, and seated it not in Rwanda itself but in Arusha, Tanzania.

Over its lifespan the tribunal indicted 93 people and secured 62 convictions before closing in 2015, including that of former prime minister Jean Kambanda, the first head of government ever convicted of genocide. It also produced the first conviction anywhere for using rape as an instrument of genocide, in the case of local official Jean-Paul Akayesu.

Eike von Repgow wrote the Sachsenspiegel around 1235 in Middle Low German rather than Latin, the language every other European law book of the era used. That choice alone made it unusual: a legal scholar's private compilation of Saxon customary law, feudal obligation and inheritance rules, written so the region's lay judges could actually read it.

It was never issued by any ruler, yet copies spread across German-speaking and Slavic lands for centuries, cited in courts long after Eike died. Illustrated manuscript versions survive with hundreds of miniature scenes of trials and punishments, making it one of the best-illustrated law codes to come out of medieval Europe.

Alfonso X of Castile wanted one law for his whole kingdom, so between roughly 1256 and 1265 his scholars produced seven books, or partidas, covering religion, government, marriage, commerce, crime and inheritance. It drew heavily on Roman and canon law, unusual for a Christian Iberian kingdom still fighting Muslim states to its south.

The code was too sweeping to enforce immediately and sat mostly unused for a century after Alfonso's death. Later Castilian kings revived it as binding law, and Spanish colonial administrators carried it across the Atlantic, where versions of the Siete Partidas shaped property and inheritance law in Louisiana and other former Spanish territories.

Athens elected Solon archon in 594 BCE because the alternative looked like civil war: poor citizens were pledging their own bodies as loan collateral and being sold into slavery when they defaulted. His seisachtheia, a Greek word meaning shaking off of burdens, wiped out existing debts and freed those already enslaved for owing money, returning some who had been sold abroad.

He also banned using a person or their family as security on any future loan, closing the trap that had caused the crisis in the first place, and capped how much land any one citizen could accumulate. He divided political rights by wealth rather than birth, which let rich commoners into offices previously reserved for aristocrats, a change later credited with opening the path toward Athenian democracy.

James Somerset had been bought in Virginia by Charles Stewart, brought to England, and had then escaped before being recaptured and put aboard a ship bound for Jamaica. Godparents from his baptism petitioned the Court of King's Bench for a writ of habeas corpus, forcing the case in front of Lord Mansfield in 1772.

Mansfield ruled narrowly, that no law positively authorised Stewart to force Somerset out of the country, and freed him on that ground alone. The public read it far more broadly, as ending slavery on English soil outright, and the ruling was seized on immediately by abolitionist campaigners on both sides of the Atlantic.

Elizabeth I's 1563 Statute of Artificers tried to fix a labour market that Tudor officials thought was slipping out of control. It fixed a seven-year minimum apprenticeship for most trades, gave justices of the peace power to set local wage ceilings each year, and made unemployment among able-bodied adults itself a punishable offence.

The statute assumed an economy where a person's trade was fixed for life and mobility between jobs was something to police rather than allow. It stayed on the books largely unchanged until 1814, when Parliament finally repealed the apprenticeship and wage-setting clauses as incompatible with an industrialising labour market.

The Black Death had killed close to a third of England's population by 1351, and survivors found their labour suddenly scarce and valuable. Landowners in Parliament responded with the Statute of Labourers, freezing wages at pre-plague rates and making it a punishable offence for a healthy peasant to refuse work or leave for a better-paying employer.

Enforcement fell to newly appointed justices of labourers, who fined and jailed workers who demanded more than the old rate. Resentment over the statute simmered for decades and fed directly into the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, when rebels marching on London singled out the statute's justices among their targets.

The Tang Code was finished in 653 CE, five hundred articles across twelve sections covering criminal justice, marriage, household registration and forced labour, drafted by officials including Zhangsun Wuji under imperial order. It graded punishment by social status and family relationship rather than treating every offender the same, so the same crime could carry different penalties depending on who committed it against whom.

Japan, Korea and Vietnam each built their own legal codes on it as they absorbed Chinese administrative practice during and after the Tang period, often translating whole articles nearly unchanged. Later Chinese dynasties kept revising rather than replacing it, so its categories still shaped Chinese law centuries after the Tang had fallen.

Eleven judges from eleven Allied nations sat on the bench in Tokyo, more than at Nuremberg, and the trial ran far longer: opening in May 1946 and not delivering verdicts until November 1948. Twenty-eight wartime Japanese leaders faced charges over the conduct of the war across Asia and the Pacific, from the invasion of China to the treatment of prisoners.

Emperor Hirohito was never charged, a decision made by General Douglas MacArthur's occupation command to keep him on the throne as a stabilising figurehead. Of the accused, seven were sentenced to death, including former prime minister Hideki Tojo, who was hanged in December 1948. One judge, India's Radhabinod Pal, dissented from the whole verdict, arguing the tribunal was victor's justice.

A defendant plunged an arm into boiling water or gripped a red-hot iron, and a priest checked the wound days later. A clean heal meant God had intervened to prove innocence; a festering one meant guilt. By around 800 the practice was standard across Frankish and English courts, administered inside churches under close clerical supervision rather than left to chance.

The ordeal survived because no better alternative existed where oaths and witnesses could not settle a case. It lasted until the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215 banned priests from taking part, cutting off the ritual's religious backing. English courts pivoted to jury trial within a few years, ending a system that had run for roughly four centuries.

Jesus faced two hearings, not one: first before the Jewish Sanhedrin at the high priest Caiaphas's residence, on a charge of blasphemy that the council could not itself carry out as a death sentence under Roman rule. He was then handed to Pontius Pilate, the Roman governor of Judaea, on the different charge of claiming kingship, which touched Roman authority directly.

Pilate is described weighing the case and offering to release a prisoner to the crowd before yielding to pressure for crucifixion, a scene historians have long treated cautiously given how the gospels were written decades later for religious rather than legal purposes. The year is not fixed with certainty; historians place it in either 30 or 33 CE, depending on how Passover dates and the length of Pilate's governorship are reconciled.

A jury of 501 Athenian citizens heard the case in 399 BCE, on charges of not recognising the city's gods and corrupting the young through his questioning. The guilty vote was close, 280 to 221, close enough that a switch of thirty votes would have acquitted him, but Athenian procedure then let the jury set the penalty itself.

Socrates could have proposed exile or a fine and likely lived, but by his own account in Plato's dialogues he mocked the court instead, comparing himself to a gadfly the city needed. The penalty vote swung harder against him than the verdict had, and he was sentenced to drink hemlock, which he did in prison, surrounded by students recording his last conversation.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu chaired the commission South Africa's new democratic government set up in 1995, and its public hearings opened the following year, first in East London. The design traded prosecution for testimony: perpetrators of apartheid-era violence could apply for amnesty by confessing their acts fully and publicly, in front of the victims or their families.

Not every application succeeded, and not every victim accepted the trade. Hearings ran for years and covered killings, torture and disappearances carried out by both the state and anti-apartheid groups. The commission's final report, delivered in 1998 with a supplementary volume in 2003, became a model other countries emerging from conflict later tried to adapt.

A Canadian law professor, John Humphrey, wrote the first draft, and a committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt argued it into its final shape across nearly two years of sessions. The United Nations General Assembly adopted the result in Paris on 10 December 1948, thirty articles covering everything from freedom of speech to the right to rest and leisure.

Eight countries abstained, including the Soviet bloc and Saudi Arabia, and none voted against it. The declaration itself binds no government; it is a statement of aspiration, not a treaty. It nonetheless became the template for dozens of later human rights treaties and national constitutions, and the date of its adoption is still marked each year as Human Rights Day.

The court that would eventually decide the boundaries of American government opened its first session on 1 February 1790 at the Royal Exchange Building in New York City, then the national capital. Chief Justice John Jay presided over five other justices, all appointed by George Washington that same year.

There was almost nothing to do. No cases had yet reached the court, and the first session mainly organised procedure and admitted lawyers to practice before it. The court would not decide its first case for another year, and it heard no case on the constitutionality of a federal law until Marbury v Madison in 1803.

Before 654, Visigothic Spain ran on two legal systems side by side: one for the Gothic conquerors, another for the Roman population they ruled. King Recceswinth's Liber Iudiciorum tore that division down, binding both peoples to the same courts and the same penalties for the first time since the kingdom's founding two centuries earlier.

The code survived the Muslim conquest of 711 largely intact, kept alive as the Liber Iudicum in territories under both Christian and Muslim rule. Its provisions on marriage, inheritance and property later fed into the Fuero Juzgo, a medieval Castilian translation that kept Recceswinth's rulings in force for another five hundred years.
